title: Hosea 12:1–14
context: Hosea sets Ephraim’s present conduct beside the story of its ancestor Jacob. Ephraim pursues treaties with Assyria and Egypt (12:1), and the LORD brings a controversy against Judah and Jacob (12:2). Hosea recalls Jacob at birth, in his wrestling, and at Bethel (12:3–5; compare Genesis 25:26, 32:24–30, and 28:10–22, and see Genesis 35:9–15). Genesis 32 speaks of “a man” and of fighting “with God”, while Hosea speaks of “the angel”; each account can be read in its own place. Hosea then calls the people to turn (12:6), indicts dishonest trade and self-satisfied wealth (12:7–8), and records the LORD’s answer from the exodus and his judgment on Gilead and Gilgal (12:9–11). Jacob’s service in Aram (12:12) is set beside the prophet by whom the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt (12:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a call to covenant faithfulness grounded in the LORD’s past dealings with Israel. Versification: English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, and English 12:1–14 is Hebrew 12:2–15; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: Ephraim feeds on wind, and chases the east wind. He continually multiplies lies and desolation. They make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried into Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says, “Ephraim feeds on wind, and chases the east wind.” Arminian readers hear a picture of empty pursuit: the northern kingdom seeks security in a covenant with Assyria while oil goes to Egypt, and the LORD holds the people responsible for these choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a foreign policy that trusts the great powers rather than the LORD; some hear the east wind as hinting at the threat from Assyria, though the line does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of misplaced trust, with “lies and desolation” as its fruit.

verses.text: The LORD also has a controversy with Judah, and will punish Jacob according to his ways; according to his deeds he will repay him.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD also has a controversy with Judah”. Arminian readers hear the language of a covenant lawsuit and the principle that the LORD repays Jacob “according to his deeds”, holding the people accountable for real choices they have made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a covenant lawsuit in which the LORD judges justly according to deeds, and Judah is not exempt. Shared ground: both traditions note that “Jacob” here names the people while recalling the ancestor, which prepares for the retelling of his story in 12:3–5.

verses.text: In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he contended with God.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the womb he took his brother by the heel” recalls Genesis 25:26, and “in his manhood he contended with God” recalls Genesis 32:24–30. Arminian readers hear Hosea using the ancestor’s story to warn his descendants: the grasping that marked Jacob marks them too, yet his story also includes seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hosea retelling Jacob’s life as a mirror for Israel. Some also recall that Genesis 25:23 stands behind Paul’s argument in Romans 9, which the Romans 9:13 box treats; Hosea’s own focus here is the people’s character. Shared ground: both traditions read Genesis and Hosea each in their own place.

verses.text: Indeed, he struggled with the angel, and prevailed; he wept, and made supplication to him. He found him at Bethel, and there he spoke with us—
verses.arminianNotes: “Indeed, he struggled with the angel, and prevailed; he wept, and made supplication to him.” Arminian readers commonly take Jacob as the one who wept and pleaded, seeing earnest prayer that sought a blessing (compare Genesis 32:26). The pronouns can be read more than one way, and Genesis 32 does not mention weeping, so this reading is best held lightly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise usually take Jacob as the one who wept and sought favor, while noting that some interpreters have read the angel as the one weeping. “He found him at Bethel” recalls Genesis 28:10–22 and 35:9–15. Shared ground: both traditions hear “there he spoke with us” as making Jacob’s encounter a word to his descendants.

verses.text: even the LORD, the God of Armies. The LORD is his name of renown!
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD is his name of renown!” Arminian readers hear the climax of the Bethel memory: the God who met Jacob is the LORD, the God of Armies, and the same God now calls Jacob’s descendants to answer him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a confession of the LORD’s name and power that ties the God of the patriarch to the God of Israel’s covenant. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grounding the call of 12:6 in who the LORD is rather than in any merit of Israel’s.

verses.text: Therefore turn to your God. Keep kindness and justice, and wait continually for your God.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore turn to your God. Keep kindness and justice, and wait continually for your God.” Arminian readers hear a sincere call that the people can answer by grace, joining repentance with the steady practice of kindness and justice. Waiting continually is itself an act of trust in the God who calls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a real command to turn, to practice kindness and justice, and to wait on God, and they add that such turning is itself the fruit of the grace the command points to. Shared ground: both traditions read repentance, ethics, and patient trust together as one response to the LORD.

verses.text: A merchant has dishonest scales in his hand. He loves to defraud.
verses.arminianNotes: “A merchant has dishonest scales in his hand. He loves to defraud.” Arminian readers see the call of 12:6 contradicted in the marketplace: the kindness and justice the LORD asks for are replaced by fraud the people choose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see dishonest trade as a breach of covenant justice, against the law’s demand for “just balances” in Leviticus 19:36. Some readers note that the Hebrew word rendered “merchant” can also mean Canaanite. Shared ground: both traditions hear the verse as showing that faithfulness to God appears in everyday dealings.

verses.text: Ephraim said, “Surely I have become rich. I have found myself wealth. In all my wealth they won’t find in me any iniquity that is sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim says, “Surely I have become rich.” Arminian readers hear self-deception: prosperity is taken as proof that “they won’t find in me any iniquity that is sin”, a boast the LORD answers in 12:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the blindness of a heart that measures itself by wealth rather than by God’s law. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that success does not prove innocence, and that self-justification is the opposite of the return called for in 12:6.

verses.text: “But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt. I will yet again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the solemn feast.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers, “But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt.” Arminian readers hear the covenant claim reasserted, with the threat to “make you dwell in tents” pointing back to the wilderness as both discipline and a chance to begin again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s covenant claim from the exodus, and many hear in “the days of the solemn feast” a recollection of the feast of booths (compare Leviticus 23:42–43), though the feast is not named here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as humbling the boast of 12:8.

verses.text: I have also spoken to the prophets, and I have multiplied visions; and by the ministry of the prophets I have used parables.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I have also spoken to the prophets, and I have multiplied visions”. Arminian readers stress that Israel was not left without warning; repeated prophetic words and parables made the people’s response a matter of real accountability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the LORD’s patient and abundant speaking through his prophets, seeing the prophetic word as his appointed means of calling and warning his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Israel’s failure did not come from any lack of revelation.

verses.text: If Gilead is wicked, surely they are worthless. In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls. Indeed, their altars are like heaps in the furrows of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: “If Gilead is wicked, surely they are worthless. In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls.” Arminian readers see worship multiplied without faithfulness, so that the altars become “like heaps in the furrows of the field”, useless piles of stone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see religious activity condemned because it is cut off from the LORD’s covenant terms. Many readers hear wordplay between Gilgal and the Hebrew word for heaps, and Gilead is also indicted at 6:8. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as judgment on worship that has become empty.

verses.text: Jacob fled into the country of Aram. Israel served to get a wife. For a wife he tended flocks and herds.
verses.arminianNotes: “Jacob fled into the country of Aram. Israel served to get a wife.” Arminian readers hear Hosea recalling Jacob’s flight and his years of service for Rachel (compare Genesis 28:5 and 29:18–20), a humble beginning set against Ephraim’s later pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the patriarch’s lowly service in a foreign land, and many hear a contrast with 12:13: Jacob kept flocks for a wife, while the LORD kept Israel by a prophet. Shared ground: both traditions read the Genesis account and Hosea’s summary of it each in their own place.

verses.text: By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.
verses.arminianNotes: “By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.” Arminian readers commonly identify the prophet as Moses, and they hear an implied call to heed the prophets now speaking, Hosea among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise commonly identify the prophet as Moses and see the LORD delivering and preserving his people through a mediator he appointed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring the prophetic word that Ephraim was despising (compare 12:10), and as the LORD’s care for Israel from the start.

verses.text: Ephraim has bitterly provoked anger. Therefore his blood will be left on him, and his Lord will repay his contempt.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim has bitterly provoked anger.” Arminian readers see judgment as the just result of persistent rebellion: “his blood will be left on him”, and the guilt is Ephraim’s own rather than imposed from outside.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Lord’s just recompense for contempt of his word, with the guilt resting on Ephraim. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing line, “his Lord will repay his contempt”, as a sober reminder that the Lord who called Israel also judges.
